publications.title: Unlocking language boundaries: AraCLIP - transforming Arabic language and image understanding through cross-lingual models
publications.abstract: In the domain of image retrieval, the integration of text and images has been transformative, facilitating models that transcend language barriers. This paper introduces Arabic Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (AraCLIP), an extension of the CLIP model tailored for Arabic image retrieval. AraCLIP leverages the CLIP architecture, introducing Knowledge Distillation to transfer cross-modal knowledge from a pre-trained English model to an Arabic counterpart.

projects/araclip.html.title: AraCLIP: Arabic Image Retrieval | Mohammad Albarham
paragraphs: Cross-lingual learning model for effective Arabic text-to-image retrieval using knowledge distillation from CLIP

AraCLIP extends the CLIP architecture for Arabic image retrieval tasks. It leverages Knowledge Distillation to transfer cross-modal knowledge from English to Arabic, enhancing its ability to understand Arabic text and retrieve relevant images.
The model outperforms state-of-the-art multilingual models by approximately 10% across various evaluation metrics including recall@1, recall@5, and mean reciprocal rank.
Transfers cross-modal knowledge from English CLIP to Arabic, preserving semantic relationships.
Specifically optimized for Arabic text understanding, not just multilingual adaptation.
10% improvement over state-of-the-art multilingual vision-language models.
Model weights and training code available on HuggingFace and GitHub.
AraCLIP uses a dual-encoder architecture with:
Text Encoder: AraBERT-based model fine-tuned for Arabic text understanding
Image Encoder: Vision Transformer (ViT) pre-trained on ImageNet
Projection Heads: Linear layers mapping both encoders to shared embedding space
The model is trained using a two-stage approach:
Stage 1: Knowledge distillation from English CLIP using parallel Arabic-English datasets
Stage 2: Fine-tuning on Arabic-specific image-caption pairs with contrastive learning

This project is a MATLAB implementation of the Structure from Motion (SfM) algorithm. The SfM algorithm is a photogrammetric range imaging technique for estimating three-dimensional structures from two-dimensional image sequences that may be coupled with local motion signals. It is studied in the fields of computer vision and visual perception. The project is implemented using MATLAB and the code is available on both Github and Mathworks. The project was a final project for Computer Vision Course at Chalmers University of Technology .

Portfoio Details

The Poetry Reader is a tool that brings Arabic poetry to life by turning written verses into natural, expressive audio. Since Arabic poetry has a unique rhythm and deep emotions, regular text-to-speech systems often sound flat and robotic. This tool solves that problem by making sure the recitation feels more human and engaging.
Making Poetry More Accessible – Helps more people enjoy and understand Arabic poetry by providing high-quality audio versions.
Preserving Cultural Heritage – Ensures the beauty and rhythm of Arabic poetry are kept alive in digital form.
Natural-Sounding Recitation – Uses smart processing to add pauses, rhythm, and tone changes, making the reading feel more like a human reciter.
Scalable and Expandable – Can grow into an educational tool for students and poetry lovers worldwide.
By carefully structuring the text before converting it into speech, the Poetry Reader creates an authentic and engaging listening experience.

projects/latest-projects-5.html.title: DINOv3-Mask2Former Urban Instance Segmentation - Mohammad Al-Barham
paragraphs: Home
Portfolio Details
Project name : Combining DINOv3 and Mask2Former for Urban Streetscapes Instance Segmentation
Course : SSY340 – Deep Machine Learning (Chalmers University) View course details
GitHub : Source code
Authors : Yinghao Chen, Mohammad Albarham
Year : 2025
Report : Project Report (PDF)
Poster : Project Poster (PDF)

This project presents a unified instance segmentation framework ( DINOv3-Mask2Former ) for urban streetscapes, developed as part of the SSY340 – Deep Machine Learning course at Chalmers University of Technology . The model integrates a self-supervised Vision Transformer ( DINOv3 ) backbone with a Mask2Former head via an enhanced ViT Adapter , forming a cohesive architecture that captures both global context and local details for robust segmentation of complex urban scenes.

Experiments on the Mapillary Vistas dataset validate the feasibility of this approach, showing that DINOv3's transferable features can be adapted for structured urban scene understanding. The model achieves strong instance segmentation performance on large objects while identifying key challenges in small and occluded instance recognition, underscoring the potential of self-supervised transformers for scalable urban perception.
Figure 1: Proposed instance segmentation architecture.
Backbone : Frozen DINOv3 pre-trained ViT-S16 extracts rich, transferable visual features.
Neck (ViT Adapter) : Custom multi-scale adapter with Conv blocks, Squeeze & Excitation modules, and cross-scale feature fusion to produce pyramid features at 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 scales.
Head (Mask2Former) : Trainable pixel decoder and mask/class heads for generating instance masks and class logits.

Trained and evaluated on the Mapillary Vistas dataset — a large-scale benchmark with 25,000 high-resolution street-level images collected worldwide. The project focused on 12 instance-level classes including Person, Car, Truck, Bus, Bicycle, Motorcycle, Traffic Sign, Street Light, Pole, Crosswalk, Driveway, and Bicyclist.
Novel integration of a frozen DINOv3-ViT backbone with a trainable Mask2Former head.
Custom multi-scale ViT Adapter with Squeeze & Excitation for cross-scale feature fusion.
Strong performance on large urban objects (vehicles, buildings).
Identified key challenges in small and occluded instance recognition.
Demonstrates the potential of self-supervised transformers for scalable urban perception tasks.

The ChatBot code creates a dialogue where users can ask questions about some aspects of memory management in C++. After the knowledge base of the chatbot has been loaded from a text file, a knowledge graph representation is created in computer memory, where chatbot answers represent the graph nodes and user queries represent the graph edges. After a user query has been sent to the chatbot, the Levenshtein distance is used to identify the most probable answer. The code is fully functional as-is and uses raw pointers to represent the knowledge graph and interconnections between objects throughout the project.

Arabic Sign Language Recognition Using Deep Learning Models

Arabic Sign Language (ArSL) is a family of sign languages that are spread throughout the Arab world. This paper focuses on developing a robust deep learning model that is trained on the ArSL2018 dataset to convert images of the ArSL alphabets into Arabic alphabets. The ArSL2018 dataset consists of 54,049 images of 32 alphabets collected from 40 signers. We have implemented and validated several deep learning models, including Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), VGG-16, and ResNet-18. The best result is attained by the modified ResNet-18 model which achieved an average test accuracy of 99.47%.

headings: PAIR — Phi's Applied and Innovative Research Program
paragraphs: Home
Resume
PAIR Program
Role Applied Researcher
Institute Phi Science Institute
Training Period February – November 2019
Location Amman, Jordan
Supported by Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Jordan
Selection Top 10% of applicants
Skills Applied Research Product Design Delft Design Approach Market Research Go-To-Market Strategy Digital Fabrication 3D Printing CNC and Laser Cutting

PAIR — Phi's Applied and Innovative Research program — integrates applied scientific research with innovation and entrepreneurship. I was selected as one of the top 10% of innovators among all candidates, and worked in a multidisciplinary team alongside business, engineering and medical students on applied projects aimed at a real market need.

The program runs over two years. Its first year is structured as four phases — problem definition, ideation and evaluation, business and marketing, and prototyping — each ending in a deliverable defended in front of a scientific committee or a panel of industry professionals. The training was held in Amman, Jordan, from February to November 2019, and was supported and funded by the Embassy of the Kingdom of the Netherlands in Jordan.
My team's outcome was Flex-mattress , a segmented hospital mattress and frame taken from problem statement through to a functional physical prototype, a CAD model and a full commercial strategy.
Scientific problem definition. Conducted qualitative market research to define a scientific problem, then wrote a research proposal and presented it to an experienced scientific committee.
Ideation and evaluation. Applied the Delft industrial design approach to move from candidate ideas to an evaluated product concept.

Business and marketing. Developed a go-to-market strategy for a hardware product — new product launch, competitive analysis, positioning, messaging and pricing — built around a unique value proposition.

Prototyping and digital fabrication. Fabricated a functional hardware prototype using 3D printing, CNC, laser cutting and moulding, and presented it with the accompanying business strategy to an array of experts and industry professionals.
Selected as one of the top 10% of innovators among all program candidates.
Defined a scientific problem from qualitative market research and defended the resulting research proposal before a scientific committee.
Applied the Delft industrial design approach to prototype a functional hardware-based product.
Formulated a comprehensive product marketing strategy introducing a unique value proposition for a hardware product in the market.
Fabricated the prototype using 3D printers, CNC, laser cutting and moulding, and presented it alongside a detailed business strategy.

Awarded a Certificate of Participation on 26 January 2020 for the nine-month Innovative Applied Research Training, covering scientific problem definition, product design, business commercialization and digital fabrication.

Organizer ICPC — International Competitive Programming Contest & the University of Jordan
Location Amman, Jordan
Technologies C++ Algorithms Data Structures Problem Solving

The JU Competitive Programming Contest (JUCPC) is the University of Jordan's qualifier within the ICPC, the International Competitive Programming Contest. Teams of three share a single machine and race to solve as many algorithmic problems as they can within a five-hour window, with a balloon delivered to the desk for every problem accepted. I competed in the 2018 edition on 6 April 2018 and again in the 2019 edition on 22 June 2019, where the contest was run under the ACPC, the Africa and Arab Collegiate Programming Championship, and I received two Certificates of Achievement.
Awarded the Extreme Programmers Certificate of Achievement at the 2019 JU Competitive Programming Contest on 22 June 2019.
Awarded a First to Solve Problem A Certificate of Achievement at the same contest, for being first in the field to get problem A accepted.
Both certificates were signed by William B. Poucher, ICPC Executive Director, and Ossama M. Ismail, ACPC Championship Director.

Also competed in JUCPC 2018 on 6 April 2018, receiving a Certificate of Participation signed by the Dean of the King Abdullah II School for Information Technology and the President of the Jordan Programmers Association.
Solved algorithmic problems in C++ under ICPC rules: three contestants to a team, one shared computer, five hours, penalty time for wrong submissions.
Organised by the University of Jordan with the Jordanian Programmers Association, the Students' Union, the Innovation and Entrepreneurship Center, and the ICPC Foundation.

Portal: FireFighting is the annual IEEE RAS robotics competition run by the IEEE RAS chapter at the University of Jordan Student Branch, giving Jordanian youth a local arena to design and build their own firefighting robot prototypes. Competing as team Electrone X with my colleague Abdullah Abu Dabaseh, we built our robots from scratch and finished 4th overall, and were also awarded the Best Design Award for the mechanical design and the Clean Sheet Award for faultless runs.
Finished 4th overall in the IEEE RAS Portal: FireFighting competition, held on 29 June 2019 at the University of Jordan.
Won the Best Design Award for the mechanical design of the robot, and the Clean Sheet Award for completing the runs without faults.
Competed as team Electrone X with my colleague Abdullah Abu Dabaseh, each of us building and running a robot of our own design.
Built the robots from scratch on a custom four-wheel chassis, with microcontroller-driven motors and a servo, a motor-driven fan to put out the flame, and laser-cut acrylic and 3D-printed parts.
Certificates signed by Prof. Lutfi Al-Sharif, IEEE RAS Jordan Chapter Chairman, and Omar Turkmani, IEEE JU RAS Chairman.
Placed 3rd with the same colleague in the previous Portal: Firefighting competition, held in October 2018.
